source: v = v₀ + at and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² hold when the acceleration is constant.
Students use these equations even when the acceleration changes partway through the motion.
When the acceleration is constant, the v–t graph is a straight line. That one fact gives the two main equations of motion, and you can read both straight off the graph.

For constant acceleration: $\role{velocity}{v} = \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_0} + \role{acceleration}{a}\role{time}{t}$ and $\role{position}{x} = \role[starting position]{position}{x_0} + \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_0} \role{time}{t} + \tfrac12 \role{acceleration}{a} \role{time}{t}^2$. They hold only while the acceleration stays the same.

A straight $v$–$t$ line starting at $v_0$ with slope $a$ has height $v_0 + at$ at time $t$: that is the first equation. The displacement is the area under that line, which splits into a rectangle ($v_0 \times t$) and a triangle on top ($\tfrac12 \times t \times at$). Adding them gives $\Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$, the second equation.
v₀ = 3 m/s and a = 2 m/s². At t = 4 s the area is 3 × 4 + ½ × 2 × 4² = 28 m.
A car at $12\ \text{m/s}$ accelerates at $2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ for $6\ \text{s}$. How fast is it going?
A train starts from rest and accelerates at $0.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ for $20\ \text{s}$. How far does it go?
A car at $20\ \text{m/s}$ brakes with $a = -5\ \text{m/s}^2$. How far does it go before it stops?
After $4\ \text{s}$ the car stays put; the equations don't apply once it has stopped.

Using these equations for a whole trip when the acceleration changes partway, like a car that speeds up and then cruises. Then $a$ is not one number, and plugging the total time into $\tfrac12 a t^2$ gives a wrong answer. Fix: split the trip where the acceleration changes; the final velocity and position of one stage are the starting values of the next.
